meta.title: Who really said "Waste no more time arguing about what a good man should be. Be one"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Genuinely Marcus Aurelius — Meditations 10.16. But the English is Maxwell Staniforth's 1964 translation, and the version online adds a word he never wrote.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Waste no more time arguing about what a good man should be. Be one'?
meta.ogDescription: Real passage, translator's words: Meditations 10.16. Staniforth's 1964 Penguin English — and the form everyone shares slips in an extra 'about'.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: The passage is real and precisely locatable: Meditations, Book 10, section 16, written in Koine Greek in Marcus’s private notebook. The famous English sentence, though, belongs to a translator — Maxwell Staniforth’s 1964 Penguin version, “Waste no more time arguing what a good man should be. Be one.” The wording that circulates online adds one word Staniforth did not use: about.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Koine Greek, c. AD 170–180, on campaign — never intended for publication
C. R. Haines, Loeb Classical Library, 1916 — public domain

source.excerpt: Put an end once for all to this discussion of what a good man should be, and be one.
trail: Wikiquote carries the familiar English — “Waste no more time arguing what a good man should be. Be one.” — in its sourced Meditations section, filed under Book X, 16 and printed alongside the Koine Greek original (Wikiquote: Marcus Aurelius ↗).

The sentence really is in the book. The public-domain 1916 Loeb translation by C. R. Haines gives 10.16 as “Put an end once for all to this discussion of what a good man should be, and be one” (Wikisource, Book 10 ↗).

The sourced-quotation site WIST files this wording as Meditations 10.16, tr. Staniforth (1964), and prints more than a dozen rival English renderings of the same Greek beside it, from Casaubon (1634) to Needleman and Piazza (2008) (WIST Quotations ↗).
Maxwell Staniforth’s translation of the Meditations was published by Penguin in 1964, which places that English text firmly inside copyright (Internet Archive catalogue record ↗).
source.excerptNote: Book 10.16 is a single free-standing sentence. Marcus wrote in short, disconnected notes, so there is no surrounding passage to quote — the entry before it is about living as a citizen of the world, the one after about picturing time as a whole. The Greek runs: “Μηκέθ᾽ ὅλως περὶ τοῦ οἷόν τινα εἶναι τὸν ἀγαθὸν ἄνδρα διαλέγεσθαι, ἀλλὰ εἶναι τοιοῦτον.” The 1916 rendering is quoted here rather than the 1964 one because it is out of copyright.

sourceLink.text: Meditations Book 10, trans. C. R. Haines (Loeb, 1916), at Wikisource

source.rightsHolder: The estate of Maxwell Staniforth (1893–1986) and Penguin Books, for the 1964 English translation
source.rightsNote: Two different clocks run here. Marcus’s Greek, written c. AD 170–180, has been in the public domain for centuries, and C. R. Haines’s 1916 Loeb translation is public domain in the United States — that is the rendering quoted above, and it may be reproduced freely. The wording people actually share, however, is Maxwell Staniforth’s Penguin translation of 1964 ↗, and a 1964 translation is a copyrighted work in its own right. Quote it as you would any modern book: briefly, and with the translator named.

author.name: Marcus Aurelius
author.heading: About Marcus Aurelius
author.metaLine: AD 121–180 · Roman emperor and Stoic philosopher
author.bio: Marcus Aurelius Antoninus ruled Rome from 161 to 180, through plague, rebellion and a long grinding war on the Danube. In whatever hours those left him he kept a private Greek notebook of Stoic self-correction — the twelve books we call the Meditations — which he almost certainly never meant anyone else to read. It is now, as Wikipedia puts it, among the most important sources for understanding ancient Stoicism, and the most quoted self-help book never written for a reader.

cite.sourceCitation: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations 10.16, in The Communings with Himself of Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, trans. C. R. Haines, Loeb Classical Library (London: William Heinemann, 1916). The widely quoted English wording — "Waste no more time arguing what a good man should be. Be one." — is from Meditations, trans. Maxwell Staniforth (Penguin Books, 1964).

misattribution.heading: Right author, borrowed words
misattribution.intro: Nobody is stealing this line from Marcus Aurelius. The trouble is subtler — the sentence everyone recognises was composed in English in 1964, and the copy in widest circulation has drifted a word away even from that.

items.why: Marcus wrote in Koine Greek and never chose an English word in his life. The crisp, shareable phrasing is one translator’s decision. Others handled the same sentence very differently — George Long (1862): “No longer talk at all about the kind of man that a good man ought to be, but be such.” A. S. L. Farquharson (1944): “Don’t any more discuss at large what the good man is like, but be good.” Gregory Hays (2003): “To stop talking about what the good man is like, and just be one.” (WIST’s translation table ↗)

The most-shared form reads “arguing about what a good man should be” — the Goodreads entry in that shape has collected thousands of likes (Goodreads ↗). The wording documented by both Wikiquote ↗ and WIST has no “about” in it, and no published translation we could locate uses that form.

The line is almost always credited to Meditations and nothing more — no book, no section, no translator. Daily Stoic’s whole page on it says only that Marcus “wrote these words in Meditations” (Daily Stoic ↗). The address is 10.16, and it takes ten seconds to check.

misattribution.truthLine: The thought is Marcus Aurelius’s beyond argument — Meditations 10.16, in his own private Greek notebook (Wikisource ↗). The English is a 1964 translator’s, and the copy in your feed has probably picked up a word neither of them wrote.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The Meditations is not a book Marcus Aurelius wrote for anyone. It is twelve books of notes to himself, composed in Greek roughly between AD 170 and 180, much of it on the Danube frontier while he was running a war and an empire; Wikipedia’s survey of the manuscript tradition notes it is unlikely he ever intended the writings to be published, and the work carries no title he gave it (Wikipedia: Meditations ↗).

That changes how 10.16 reads. It is not advice dispensed from a throne to an audience of philosophy students. It is the most powerful man in the world catching himself mid-rumination and cutting it off. The imperative is aimed inward — which is exactly why it survives being lifted onto a poster, and exactly what the poster tends to lose.
detailsBody: The line’s modern punch is largely an artefact of modern English. Jeremy Collier in 1701 rendered the same Greek as a small essay — “Notion without Practice is Impertinence; spend no more time then in stating the Qualifications of a Man of Virtue, but endeavour to get them.” Gerald Rendall in 1898 got closer to the modern snap: “No more mere talk of what the good man should be. Be it!” Martin Hammond in 2006: “No more roundabout discussion of what makes a good man. Be one!” (all as collected by WIST ↗).

So the sentence people quote is a genuine collaboration across eighteen centuries: Marcus supplied the thought, and a twentieth-century English clergyman-translator supplied the two-word ending that makes it land. Both deserve the credit, and only one of them usually gets it.
context.pull: He was not telling anyone else to stop arguing. He was telling himself.
